lessons.title: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Laws
lessons.body:
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) laws make companies that make or sell products responsible for the waste those products become. In Africa, South Africa leads with EPR regulations under the National Environmental Management: Waste Act (Act 59 of 2008). Since 2021, producers of paper, packaging, electrical equipment, and lighting must join a Producer Responsibility Organisation (PRO) and pay fees based on tonnage. For example, a company putting 100 tonnes of packaging on the market pays around R500âR1,500 per tonne to a PRO like PETCO or Polyco. That money funds collection and recycling.

As a recycler or green entrepreneur, EPR creates opportunities. You can register as a collection or processing partner with a PRO. PROs need reliable collectors to meet targets: South Africa aims to recycle 70% of packaging by 2025. In Kenya, the Sustainable Waste Management Act 2022 also introduces EPR. Kenyaâs PROs, such as the Kenya Extended Producer Responsibility Organization (KEPRO), are recruiting waste pickers and small recyclers. To benefit, register your business, keep records of tonnage collected, and invoice the PRO. You can earn R500âR2,000 per tonne for sorted PET plastic, for example.

To start, contact the PRO in your country. In South Africa, visit the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) website for a list of registered PROs. In Kenya, check the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA). Ask about their collection network and payment rates. You will need a simple contract, a way to weigh materials (a scale), and transport. Many PROs also offer training and equipment grants. EPR is not just regulationâit is a funding stream for your recycling business.

lessons.title: Waste Reduction Legislation: Bans and Mandates
lessons.body:
Many African countries have passed laws to ban or restrict certain waste streams. Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008 and later single-use plastics. Kenya banned plastic bags in 2017 and single-use plastics in national parks in 2020. These bans create demand for alternatives like cloth bags, paper bags, and reusable containers. For example, in Rwanda, entrepreneurs making woven baskets and cloth bags have grown. In Kenya, a ban on plastic bags led to a boom in eco-friendly packaging businesses.

Bans also affect recyclers. If a material is banned, you cannot collect it for recyclingâbut you can collect it for safe disposal or transformation. For instance, Rwandaâs plastic ban means PET bottles are still allowed, but thin plastic bags are not. So recycling PET bottles remains viable. In South Africa, there is no national plastic bag ban, but a plastic bag levy (currently R32 per kilogram) encourages reuse and recycling. The levy funds the recycling of bags through PROs.

Mandates are another tool. Some countries require households and businesses to separate waste at source. In South Africa, the National Waste Management Strategy 2020 mandates separation of recyclables in certain municipalities. In Kenya, the Sustainable Waste Management Act 2022 requires segregation into organic, recyclable, and hazardous waste. For your business, this means you can offer collection services for separated waste. You can also partner with municipalities to set up drop-off centres.

To take advantage, know the laws in your area. Check your national environmental authority website. If a ban is coming, pivot your business to banned material alternatives or safe disposal. If segregation is mandated, offer collection and sorting services. For example, in Nairobi, TakaTaka Solutions collects segregated waste from offices and earns from recycling. Legislation is not a barrierâit is a market signal.

lessons.title: International Recycling Policies and Agreements
lessons.body:
International agreements affect what happens to waste in Africa. The Basel Convention controls transboundary movements of hazardous waste. In 2019, the Basel Ban Amendment entered into force, prohibiting developed countries from exporting hazardous waste to developing countries. This includes mixed plastic waste that is hard to recycle. As a result, countries like Ghana and Nigeria now receive less low-quality plastic waste, but also face challenges in managing their own waste. For your business, this means more local plastic is available for recyclingâgood news if you process plastic.

The Bamako Convention is an African treaty that bans the import of hazardous waste into Africa. It has been ratified by many African Union countries. It reinforces the Basel Ban. If you see suspicious waste imports, you can report them to your national authority. The convention also encourages African countries to develop their own recycling capacity.

The Paris Agreement on climate change drives national policies that support recycling. Many African countries include waste management in their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). For example, South Africaâs NDC includes reducing waste to landfill and increasing recycling. This can unlock climate finance for recycling projects. You can apply for grants from the Green Climate Fund or the Global Environment Facility through local partners.

The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), push governments to improve waste management. Many donors fund recycling projects that align with SDGs. To benefit, align your business with these goals in grant applications. For instance, a project that recycles plastic and creates jobs for youth can attract funding from the African Development Bank or UNDP. Stay informed by following the Basel Convention website and your countryâs environment ministry.

lessons.title: Advocacy Skills: Lobbying for Circular Economy Policies
lessons.body:
Advocacy is about influencing policies that affect your recycling business. You can lobby local councillors, members of parliament, or ministry officials. Start by building a clear case. For example, show that recycling creates jobs: in South Africa, the waste sector employs over 60,000 people, many in recycling. In Kenya, the informal waste sector employs over 100,000 people. Use these numbers to argue for better support.

Join or form a coalition. There is strength in numbers. In South Africa, the South African Waste Pickers Association (SAWPA) advocates for waste picker rights. In Kenya, the Kenya National Waste Pickers Welfare Association does similar work. If you are a small recycler, join a local business association or an environmental NGO. Together, you can request meetings with officials. Prepare a one-page brief with your key asks: e.g., reduce licensing fees, provide land for sorting, or enforce separation-at-source laws.

Use the media. Write a press release or invite journalists to your site. A story about how your recycling business reduces pollution and creates jobs can pressure policymakers. Social media works too: tag your local government and use hashtags like #CircularEconomyAfrica. In 2021, Kenyan activists used Twitter to push for the Sustainable Waste Management Act. 

Attend public participation meetings. In many African countries, new laws require public comment. For example, South Africaâs EPR regulations had a public comment period. You can submit written comments or speak at hearings. Even if you are not an expert, your practical experience matters. Tell them what works on the ground. Finally, follow up. Advocacy is a long game. Build relationships with officials over time. Offer to sit on a municipal waste forum. Your voice can shape policies that help your business grow.

lessons.title: Compliance with Environmental Regulations
lessons.body:
If you run a recycling business, you must comply with environmental regulations. In South Africa, you need a waste management licence from the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) if you store, treat, or dispose of waste. For small recyclers, a basic licence may cost around R2,000âR5,000 and take 3â6 months. In Kenya, you need an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) licence from NEMA. Fees vary but can be KSh 10,000â50,000 for small operations. 

Start by registering your business. In South Africa, register with the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC). In Kenya, register with the Business Registration Service. Then apply for environmental permits. You will need to show how you handle waste, emissions, and wastewater. For example, if you wash plastic, you must manage the wastewaterâdo not dump it into rivers. Build a simple settling pond or connect to a sewer. 

Keep records. Inspectors can visit anytime. Maintain a log of waste received, processed, and sold. Record the weight (use a scale) and the buyer. In South Africa, you must report annually to the DFFE if you handle more than 10 tonnes per month. In Kenya, NEMA requires annual environmental audits. Fines for non-compliance can be steep: up to R10 million in South Africa or KSh 2 million in Kenya. 

Get help. Many municipalities have small business support desks. The National Cleaner Production Centre in South Africa offers free assessments. In Kenya, the Kenya Industrial Research and Development Institute (KIRDI) can advise. Also, join a recycling associationâthey often provide compliance templates. Compliance may seem like a burden, but it builds trust with buyers and PROs. Many PROs only work with licensed recyclers. So, it is an investment in your business.

lessons.title: The Role of Local Government in Recycling
lessons.body:
Local governmentâmunicipalities and county governmentsâis key to recycling. They are responsible for waste collection and disposal. In many African cities, local authorities collect only 40â60% of waste. The rest is dumped or burned. This is a gap you can fill. For example, in Accra, Ghana, the Zoomlion company works with the city to collect waste. In Nairobi, Kenya, the county government licenses private waste collectors.

You can partner with your local government. Offer to collect recyclables from markets, schools, or offices. In South Africa, municipalities must have Integrated Waste Management Plans (IWMPs). These plans often include recycling targets. You can ask to see the plan and align your business with it. For instance, if the plan aims to divert 50% of waste from landfill, propose a collection scheme for PET bottles. 

Local governments can also provide land. Many have transfer stations or landfill sites where you can set up a sorting facility. In Durban, South Africa, the city supports waste pickers at the Bisasar Road landfill. In Kenya, counties are required to establish material recovery facilities (MRFs). You can bid to operate one. 

They also enforce bylaws. For example, a bylaw may require households to separate waste. If enforced, it guarantees you a steady supply of clean recyclables. You can report non-separation to the local authority. 

To engage, attend council meetings. Get to know the environmental officer or waste management officer. Offer a proposal: âWe will collect recyclables from 100 households weekly for a fee, reducing your landfill costs.â Show the financial benefit: landfill costs municipalities money per tonne. In South Africa, landfill costs R300âR500 per tonne. If you divert waste, you save them money. That is a strong argument. Local government is not just a regulatorâit can be your biggest client.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Policy, Regulation, and Advocacy for African Recycling Businesses

For an African recycling or green business, policy is not background noise â it is the operating environment. Your licence to collect waste, your ability to export processed material, your eligibility for tax incentives, and your freedom to operate in a municipal dumpsite all depend on the regulatory framework around you. This practical reference consolidates the rules, instruments, and advocacy tactics that matter most to recyclers and circular-economy enterprises across the continent. It is written business-first: every section tells you what to check, what to document, and what to do.

1. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Laws

EPR shifts the cost and responsibility for end-of-life products onto producers, packers, and importers. For recyclers, EPR is a revenue channel: producers must pay fees to Producer Responsibility Organisations (PROs), which then contract collection and processing capacity. South Africa's EPR regulations under the National Environmental Management: Waste Act (Act 59 of 2008), as amended in 2020, are the most mature on the continent. They cover paper, packaging, electrical and electronic equipment, and lighting. Producers must join a PRO, pay fees, and meet collection and recycling targets.

Kenya's Sustainable Waste Management Act (2022) mandates EPR for all products and packaging and requires producers to establish or join a PRO. Nigeria's National Environmental (Electrical/Electronic Sector) Regulations (2011) and the EPR guidelines issued by NESREA require electronics producers to register and finance take-back. Ghana's National Environment (Mining, Quarrying and Salt Mining) Regulations are less relevant to recyclers, but Ghana's draft EPR framework for plastics and e-waste is advancing. Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania have EPR provisions in their waste laws, though implementation varies.

Business action: Register as a service provider with every PRO operating in your materials stream. PROs publish tenders for collection, sorting, and processing. Keep audited tonnage records â EPR fee calculations and target verification depend on verifiable data. If you process e-waste, ensure your facility meets the technical standards referenced in the regulations, because PRO contracts increasingly require independent audits.

2. Waste Reduction Legislation: Bans and Mandates

Bans and mandates create demand for recyclers and constrain them simultaneously. Rwanda banned single-use plastic bags in 2008 and later restricted single-use plastics; Kenya banned single-use plastic bags in 2017 and single-use plastics in protected areas in 2020. These bans reduce feedstock for plastic recyclers but also push producers toward recyclable alternatives and create enforcement-related collection opportunities.

Mandates are more directly useful. South Africa's EPR targets are mandatory. Kenya's Sustainable Waste Management Act requires segregation at source for waste generators and establishes a deposit-refund scheme for certain containers. Nigeria's Extended Producer Responsibility guidelines require producers to meet recovery targets. Several countries mandate public procurement of recycled-content products, which creates a guaranteed market â for example, recycled paper, plastic lumber, and compost.

Business action: Map bans and mandates against your feedstock. If a ban removes your input, pivot to materials that remain legal and in demand. If a mandate creates a market (recycled-content procurement, deposit-refund), position your product as compliant. Document compliance with any recycled-content or segregation requirements, because buyers increasingly ask for proof.

3. International Recycling Policies and Agreements

The Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal is the single most important international instrument for African recyclers. The 2019 amendments (effective 2021) brought most mixed and contaminated plastic waste under the Convention's control, requiring prior informed consent for exports. The Bamako Convention, adopted by African states in 1991 and in force since 1998, bans the import of hazardous waste into Africa, including radioactive waste, and regulates transboundary movement within the continent.

The Basel Convention's e-waste amendments and the Partnership for Action on Computing Equipment (PACE) affect electronics recyclers. The Minamata Convention on Mercury affects lamp and battery recyclers. The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol phases down hydrofluorocarbons and creates opportunities in refrigerant recovery and reclamation.

Business action: If you export processed material, verify that your shipment complies with Basel prior informed consent procedures and that your importing partner holds the necessary permits. If you import feedstock, confirm it is not classified as hazardous waste under Basel or prohibited under Bamako. Non-compliance can result in seizure, fines, and criminal liability. Use the Basel Convention's e-learning and notification tools, and consult your national focal point before shipping.

4. Advocacy Skills: Lobbying for Circular Economy Policies

African recyclers often operate in policy environments written without them. Advocacy is therefore a core business skill, not a public-relations add-on. The most effective advocacy is evidence-based, coalition-built, and framed around jobs, tax revenue, and municipal cost savings â not only environmental benefits.

Practical steps:

  • Build a data file: tonnages collected, jobs created, taxes paid, landfill diversion, and cost per tonne compared with municipal collection. This is your credibility.
  • Join or form an industry association: the South African Waste Pickers Association, the African Circular Economy Alliance, and national recycling associations give you collective voice and access to consultations.
  • Engage at the right level: national treasury and environment ministries for tax and EPR; municipal councils for bylaws, land, and collection contracts.
  • Use formal channels: written submissions on draft regulations, public hearings, and parliamentary committee appearances. Informal meetings help but do not replace the record.
  • Frame asks precisely: a specific tax rebate, a defined procurement quota, a streamlined permit, or a designated collection zone. Vague requests get vague responses.

Business action: Assign one person to track policy consultations. Diarise submission deadlines. Keep a one-page company profile with your metrics ready for meetings. Partner with NGOs and academic institutions on research that supports your position.

5. Compliance with Environmental Regulations

Compliance is a licence to operate and a competitive advantage when tendering for PRO or corporate contracts. Core obligations across most African jurisdictions include environmental impact assessment (EIA) or environmental audit for processing facilities, waste management licences, effluent and air emission permits, hazardous waste handling and storage rules, and occupational health and safety requirements.

Key instruments include South Africa's National Environmental Management Act (Act 107 of 1998) and the Waste Act, Kenya's Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act (EMCA, 1999) and Sustainable Waste Management Act (2022), Nigeria's NESREA Act and regulations, and Ghana's Environmental Protection Agency Act (Act 490). Many countries require annual environmental audits and public disclosure.

Table 1: Selected African EPR and waste policy instruments relevant to recyclers
Country Instrument Year Key implication for recyclers
South Africa EPR Regulations under NEM:WA 2020 Mandatory PRO membership for producers; contracts for collectors and processors
Kenya Sustainable Waste Management Act 2022 EPR for all products and packaging; source segregation; deposit-refund schemes
Nigeria NESREA EPR Guidelines 2014â2021 Producer registration and recovery targets; e-waste take-back
Rwanda Law on Environment and plastic ban 2008/2019 Restrictions on single-use plastics; demand for alternatives and recovery
Ghana EPA Act and draft EPR framework 1994/ongoing Emerging EPR obligations for plastics and e-waste

Sources: South African Government Gazette No. 43879 (2020); Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 42 (2022); NESREA EPR Guidelines (2014â2021); Rwanda Official Gazette (2008, 2019); Ghana EPA (1994) and draft EPR framework.

Table 2: Compliance obligations checklist by business activity
Activity Typical permit / obligation Issuing authority (examples)
Waste collection and transport Waste carrier licence; vehicle standards National environment agency; municipal waste department
Sorting and processing facility EIA or environmental audit; waste management licence; air/effluent permits National environment agency; local government
Hazardous / e-waste handling Hazardous waste licence; storage and labelling rules; export permits National environment agency; Basel Convention focal point
Export of recyclables Prior informed consent; customs and shipping documentation National focal point; customs authority
Employment and operations OSH registration; waste worker safety compliance; tax registration Labour ministry; revenue authority

Sources: UNEP (2021), Extended Producer Responsibility: A Guidance Manual for African Countries; Basel Convention Secretariat, Technical Guidelines on Transboundary Movements of E-Waste (2019); national environmental management acts of South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana.

â ï¸ SAFETY AND LEGAL WARNING

Do not ship, store, or process hazardous waste â including e-waste, batteries, lamps, and contaminated plastics â without the required national permits and, where applicable, Basel Convention prior informed consent. Illegal transboundary shipments can result in seizure of goods, heavy fines, and criminal prosecution. African ports and customs authorities increasingly screen for e-waste and mixed plastic waste. Verify the classification of every export consignment with your national Basel focal point before it leaves your facility. Keep hazardous waste separate from general recyclables at all times, and train workers on handling and emergency procedures.

6. The Role of Local Government in Recycling

In most African countries, local government controls the practical levers: land for sorting and processing, collection routes and schedules, dumpsite access, bylaws on waste segregation, and local procurement. Metropolitan authorities such as Nairobi City County, Lagos State, Accra Metropolitan Assembly, and City of Cape Town have dedicated waste departments and, in some cases, circular economy strategies.

Business action: Build a working relationship with your municipal waste department. Understand the Integrated Development Plan or equivalent, and align your service offering with it. Bid for collection contracts, apply for land leases for sorting facilities, and propose public-private partnerships. Local bylaws on mandatory segregation create cleaner feedstock for your operations â advocate for them and comply with them.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Register with every PRO operating in your material streams and keep audited tonnage records.
  • Map all bans, mandates, and EPR targets affecting your feedstock and products.
  • Verify Basel/Bamako compliance before any export or import of recyclable material.
  • Maintain a current environmental licence, EIA/audit, and hazardous waste permits.
  • Keep a one-page advocacy profile with jobs, tonnages, taxes, and landfill diversion data.
  • Track policy consultations and submit written comments before deadlines.
  • Build a formal relationship with your municipal waste department and understand its plans.
  • Train workers on hazardous waste handling and keep safety data sheets on site.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Basel Convention â Plastic Waste Amendments and Guidance
  • UNEP â Extended Producer Responsibility: A Guidance Manual for African Countries
  • South Africa Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment â EPR Regulations
  • Kenya National Environment Management Authority â Waste and EPR Resources
  • Nigeria NESREA â Environmental Regulations and EPR Guidelines

quiz.q: What does Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) require?
options: A) Producers pay for the waste their products become
B) Consumers pay a tax on all products
D) Recyclers pay producers for waste
quiz.explanation: EPR makes producers responsible for the end-of-life of their products, often through fees paid to PROs.

quiz.q: In South Africa, which organisation do producers join under EPR regulations?
quiz.explanation: Producers must join a PRO, which collects fees and funds recycling.

quiz.q: How can a small recycler benefit from EPR?
options: B) By registering as a collection partner with a PRO
quiz.explanation: PROs need collection partners and pay per tonne, creating income for recyclers.

quiz.q: Which country banned plastic bags in 2017?
quiz.explanation: Kenya banned plastic bags in 2017, with later bans on single-use plastics in parks.

quiz.q: What is a mandate in waste legislation?
options: B) A requirement to separate waste at source
quiz.explanation: Mandates require actions like waste separation, creating opportunities for collection services.

quiz.q: What does the Basel Ban Amendment prohibit?
options: A) Export of hazardous waste from developed to developing countries
B) Import of recyclables into Africa
quiz.explanation: The Basel Ban Amendment stops hazardous waste exports, including mixed plastics, to developing countries.

quiz.q: Which African treaty bans hazardous waste imports?
quiz.explanation: The Bamako Convention is an African treaty that bans hazardous waste imports into Africa.

quiz.q: How can the Paris Agreement support recycling businesses?
options: B) By providing climate finance for recycling projects
quiz.explanation: Many NDCs include waste management, unlocking climate finance for recycling.

quiz.q: What is a key advocacy action for recyclers?
options: B) Joining a coalition or association
quiz.explanation: Coalitions amplify voices and are more effective in lobbying for policy changes.

quiz.q: In South Africa, what licence do you need to store or treat waste?
options: A) Waste management licence from DFFE
quiz.explanation: A waste management licence from DFFE is required for waste storage, treatment, or disposal.

quiz.q: What is the penalty for non-compliance with environmental regulations in South Africa?
options: A) Up to R10 million fine
quiz.explanation: Fines can reach R10 million for serious non-compliance.

quiz.q: How can local government support recycling?
options: A) By providing land for sorting facilities
C) By increasing landfill fees only
quiz.explanation: Local governments can provide land, contracts, and enforcement of separation bylaws.

quiz.q: What is an Integrated Waste Management Plan (IWMP)?
options: A) A municipal plan that includes recycling targets
B) A national ban on plastic
quiz.explanation: IWMPs are municipal plans that often set recycling and diversion targets.

quiz.q: In Kenya, which authority issues EIA licences?
quiz.explanation: NEMA (National Environment Management Authority) issues EIA licences in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is a practical way to advocate for circular economy policies?
options: A) Submit comments on draft regulations
quiz.explanation: Public comment periods allow recyclers to influence policies with practical input.

quiz.q: Which SDG is most directly linked to recycling?
options: A) SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production
quiz.explanation: SDG 12 promotes sustainable waste management and recycling.

quiz.q: What does the South African plastic bag levy fund?
options: A) Recycling of bags through PROs
quiz.explanation: The levy funds recycling initiatives, often via PROs.

quiz.q: How can a recycler partner with local government?
options: A) Offer to collect recyclables from markets or offices
quiz.explanation: Partnerships to collect recyclables can reduce municipal landfill costs and provide steady supply.

quiz.q: What is the Bamako Convention?
options: A) An African treaty banning hazardous waste imports
quiz.explanation: The Bamako Convention bans hazardous waste imports into Africa.

quiz.q: What record-keeping is required for compliance?
options: A) Log of waste received, processed, and sold
quiz.explanation: Inspectors require detailed logs of waste quantities and transactions.

quiz.q: Which Kenyan law introduced EPR?
options: B) Environmental Management and Coordination Act
quiz.explanation: The Sustainable Waste Management Act 2022 includes EPR provisions in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of joining a recycling association?
options: A) Compliance templates and advocacy support
quiz.explanation: Associations provide resources and collective advocacy for members.

quiz.q: How does separation-at-source mandate help recyclers?
quiz.explanation: Separation ensures recyclables are not contaminated, increasing their value.

quiz.q: What is the role of a PRO?
options: A) Collect fees from producers and fund recycling
quiz.explanation: PROs manage EPR fees and support collection and recycling infrastructure.

quiz.q: In South Africa, which department oversees waste management licences?
quiz.explanation: The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) issues waste licences.

quiz.q: What is a practical advocacy tool for recyclers?
quiz.explanation: Social media can raise awareness and pressure policymakers.

quiz.q: How can local government bylaws help recyclers?
options: A) Enforce waste separation, ensuring supply
quiz.explanation: Bylaws that mandate separation guarantee a steady stream of recyclables.

quiz.q: What is the Basel Convention?
options: A) An international treaty controlling transboundary hazardous waste
C) A PRO in South Africa
quiz.explanation: The Basel Convention regulates the movement of hazardous waste across borders.

quiz.q: What support can municipalities offer to recyclers?
quiz.explanation: Many municipalities provide land or access to transfer stations for sorting.

quiz.q: Why is compliance important for working with PROs?
options: A) PROs often require licensed recyclers
C) PROs pay more to unlicensed recyclers
quiz.explanation: PROs prefer to partner with licensed, compliant recyclers to meet their targets.
